entries.title: Bankers Life Insurance Co. of Nebraska v. Alyucan Interstate Corp. (In re Alyucan Interstate Corp.), 12 B.R. 803 (Bankr. D. Utah 1981)
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: No. Judge Mabey denied stay relief: protection concerns value of lien/property interest, not a fixed buffer ratio or accrued but unpaid interest. Since real property value stable and secured recoverability unaffected, collateral adequately protected without new cash/remedies; property essential to rehabilitation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Adequate protection §361/§362(d)(1) preserves recoverable lien value against stay-related decline, not necessarily a specific 'equity cushion' balance from interest accrual; a cushion can be evidentiary but is not indispensable.
entries.legalExplanation: Court rejected mechanical cushion test on four grounds: inconsistent with preservation (not cushion preservation) purpose of AP, §§361(1)-(3) allow payments/replacement liens/indubitable equivalents not defined by margin, §362(d)(2) expressly asks absence of equity PLUS lack of reorganization necessity, and pre-Code stay litigation used holistic case-specific factors. Bankruptcy aims breathing spell against creditor scramble; AP is interim palliative rather than cure for all creditor problems. Even sizable cushion need not be frozen against interest-driven erosion absent threat to lien value. It remains useful EVIDENCE of stability and can itself protect against depreciation for period.
entries.examApplication: Use exact facts stable $1.425m value, ~$1.297m filing debt increasing to ~$1.331m, declining cushion ~$127,774→$94,239, no property depreciation; distinguish an actual decline that impairs security.
entries.examTrap: Alyucan does NOT state equity cushion always irrelevant or that secured creditor cannot get AP when collateral actually loses value.
entries.sourceRole: Full judicial opinion excerpted in uploaded Chapter 7
entries.facts: Construction/real-estate developer Alyucan filed Chapter11 Jan.14,1981. Bankers Life held first deed of trust securing original principal ~$1.22m. At filing realty worth $1,425,000, debt $1,297,226, leaving cushion $127,774 (~9% of collateral). On May stay hearing value STILL $1,425,000, but accumulating interest (~$8k/month) raised debt to $1,330,761, reducing equity cushion to $94,239 (~6.5%). Creditor argued eroding cushion required protection and relief; property was essential to the debtor's proposed reorganization.
entries.issue: Does §362(d)(1) require preserving a secured lender's equity cushion against postpetition interest accrual even when collateral has not declined and lien value is not impaired?
entries.holding: No. Judge Mabey denied stay relief: protection concerns value of lien/property interest, not a fixed buffer ratio or accrued but unpaid interest. Since real property value stable and secured recoverability unaffected, collateral adequately protected without new cash/remedies; property essential to rehabilitation.
entries.reasoning: Court rejected mechanical cushion test on four grounds: inconsistent with preservation (not cushion preservation) purpose of AP, §§361(1)-(3) allow payments/replacement liens/indubitable equivalents not defined by margin, §362(d)(2) expressly asks absence of equity PLUS lack of reorganization necessity, and pre-Code stay litigation used holistic case-specific factors. Bankruptcy aims breathing spell against creditor scramble; AP is interim palliative rather than cure for all creditor problems. Even sizable cushion need not be frozen against interest-driven erosion absent threat to lien value. It remains useful EVIDENCE of stability and can itself protect against depreciation for period.
entries.rule: Adequate protection §361/§362(d)(1) preserves recoverable lien value against stay-related decline, not necessarily a specific 'equity cushion' balance from interest accrual; a cushion can be evidentiary but is not indispensable.

entries.title: Four explicit reasons for rejecting automatic cushion-based relief
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: (1) Misstates lien-value purpose; (2) disregards flexible §361 money/substitute lien alternatives; (3) undermines separate two-prong §362(d)(2); (4) ignores historical multi-factor stay practice.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't get relief just because arbitrary 10% buffer shrank to 6.5%.
entries.legalExplanation: Court preferred responsive valuation of actual protected lien instead of predetermined percentage threshold.
entries.examApplication: Professor can ask each rationale separately—memorize all four.
entries.examTrap: Rejecting mechanical cushion is different from claiming a cushion never provides factual AP.

entries.title: Cushion may be sufficient but is not necessary
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: An adequate equity buffer may absorb depreciation; no cushion is required if alternative protection preserves lien value or stable collateral supports all secured rights.
entries.laymanExplanation: Collateral can stay safe with cash payments or extra collateral even if original buffer vanished.
entries.legalExplanation: §361 enumerates flexible substitutes beyond original property; §362(d)(2) tests equity for DIFFERENT purpose.
entries.examApplication: Compare no-cushion-but-protected case with positive-cushion-rapid-depreciation case.
entries.examTrap: Don't confuse §362(d)(2)'s debtor equity inquiry with §362(d)(1)'s lender protection.

entries.title: Separate book's unresolved postpetition interest question from holding
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: Casebook asks whether lender's prospective §506(b) interest expectation is part of property interest and whether a declining COLLATERAL value that erodes cushion differs from interest-only erosion; opinion expressly decided stable property with interest-driven debt growth.
entries.laymanExplanation: The harder future scenario is property actually falling, not only debt growing.
entries.legalExplanation: Timbers later clarifies §506(a)/(b) interrelation; exact edges depend value/date.
entries.examApplication: Treat question as analytical discussion not answered automatically by 'no cushion preservation'.
entries.examTrap: Book inquiry is not a new court holding.

entries.title: No §362(d)(2) relief when needed property and cushion/equity remain
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: Court observed debtor had equity and property essential to reorganization, so alternative §362(d)(2) no-equity-plus-unnecessary requirements not met.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bank couldn't take building simply because expected interest would consume spare equity later.
entries.legalExplanation: Two subsections address different harms: (d)(1) lender value and (d)(2) estate bankruptcy purpose.
entries.examApplication: In fact-pattern apply each subsection independently.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply lost opportunity cost as 'cause' after Timbers.

entries.title: §362 requires contextual, ad hoc remedy during reorganization
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: Interim AP court should weigh stability, forecast, necessity, alternatives and risk instead of rote formula, allowing operations while protecting security value.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judge shouldn't decide all cases just from loan-to-value ratio.
entries.legalExplanation: Mabey described AP as flexible balance to preserve business opportunity and avoid chaotic races.
entries.examApplication: Use specific financial evidence/anticipated plan stage.
entries.examTrap: No blanket right to free collateral consumption when likely decline is shown.

topics.title: B.2 United Savings v. Timbers — Full Supreme Court Case Brief
topics.description: Unanimous no compensation for undersecured creditor's delay in foreclosure; statutory holistic reading.

entries.title: United Savings Association of Texas v. Timbers of Inwood Forest Associates, Ltd., 484 U.S. 365 (1988)
entries.page: Ch.7 §B.2 / Timbers full Supreme Court opinion
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: No. Unanimous Supreme Court (Scalia) affirmed Fifth Circuit: adequate protection guards value of lien against decline; does not include lost opportunity to foreclose/reinvest, so undersecured lender receives no interim opportunity-cost or postpetition interest under §362(d)(1).
entries.laymanExplanation: An undersecured lender is NOT entitled to §361/§362(d)(1) AP compensation for opportunity cost of not foreclosing during case; only threatened decline in lien's collateral value protected, while plan confirmation PV is separate.
entries.legalExplanation: Scalia interpreted whole Code: (1) §506(a) creditor interest means collateral value, not immediate possession opportunity; (2) §506(b)/§502(b)(2) carefully restrict postpetition interest to oversecured cushion, so detour through AP would subvert distinction; (3) §552(b) restricts lender entitlement to postpetition rents/profits to properly perfected prepetition security interest, which opportunity-interest theory would evade; (4) §362(d)(2) no-equity AND lack of effective reorganization necessity would be rendered absurd/superfluous if all undersecured lenders could demand stay interest under (d)(1). Creditor protected if project actually depreciates, but no hypothetical investment income; §1129 plan present-value payment is distinct future confirmation obligation. Dictum: debtor must show realistic possibility of successful reorganization in reasonable time under (d)(2).
entries.examApplication: Write §506(b), §552(b) and §362(d)(2) structural arguments, and explain lender's demand for 12% on $4.25m versus stable apartment value.
entries.examTrap: Timbers doesn't say all deferred PLAN payments may be interest-free, or secured lender cannot demand compensation for actual collateral depreciation.
entries.sourceRole: Full judicial opinion excerpted in uploaded Chapter 7
entries.facts: On June29 1982, Texas apartment developer borrowed $4.1m against Houston apartment project with assignment of rents. Chapter11 filed March4 1985. United Savings owed $4,366,388.77, and collateral valued between $2.65m and $4.25m, only slight appreciation; lender UNDERSECURED. After March18 stay-relief motion, lender argued stay deprived immediate foreclosure value and market return. Bankruptcy judge required 12% annual market-rate payments on assumed $4.25m foreclosure recovery starting six months after filing, but Fifth Circuit en banc reversed. Supreme Court reviewed solely (d)(1) AP opportunity cost, not separate (d)(2) request.
entries.issue: Does §362(d)(1) 'adequate protection of an interest in property' entitle an UNDERsecured creditor to market-rate compensation for delay in seizing and reinvesting collateral, despite stable property value?
entries.holding: No. Unanimous Supreme Court (Scalia) affirmed Fifth Circuit: adequate protection guards value of lien against decline; does not include lost opportunity to foreclose/reinvest, so undersecured lender receives no interim opportunity-cost or postpetition interest under §362(d)(1).
entries.reasoning: Scalia interpreted whole Code: (1) §506(a) creditor interest means collateral value, not immediate possession opportunity; (2) §506(b)/§502(b)(2) carefully restrict postpetition interest to oversecured cushion, so detour through AP would subvert distinction; (3) §552(b) restricts lender entitlement to postpetition rents/profits to properly perfected prepetition security interest, which opportunity-interest theory would evade; (4) §362(d)(2) no-equity AND lack of effective reorganization necessity would be rendered absurd/superfluous if all undersecured lenders could demand stay interest under (d)(1). Creditor protected if project actually depreciates, but no hypothetical investment income; §1129 plan present-value payment is distinct future confirmation obligation. Dictum: debtor must show realistic possibility of successful reorganization in reasonable time under (d)(2).
entries.rule: An undersecured lender is NOT entitled to §361/§362(d)(1) AP compensation for opportunity cost of not foreclosing during case; only threatened decline in lien's collateral value protected, while plan confirmation PV is separate.
entries.notes: Court explicitly did not rule on §362(d)(2) as lender had not sought that separate relief; feasibility test was dictum. Single asset real estate §362(d)(3) enacted afterward may demand interest payments.

entries.title: Timbers's key distinction: protected property value versus delayed seizure right
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: Secured party's lien is property interest; right to IMMEDIATE foreclosure and investment return isn't a value dimension safeguarded by adequate protection. Actual collateral decline is safeguarded.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bank protected against apartment depreciation, not inability to invest foreclosure check.
entries.legalExplanation: Under Chapter11 temporary stay, property may continue serving enterprise though lender cannot exercise collection now.
entries.examApplication: Frame issue as time value of delayed foreclosure, not abstract whether interest ever due.
entries.examTrap: If value of apartment did decline materially, court said §361 could require cash or replacement security.

entries.title: Holistic §506(a)/(b) and §502(b)(2) argument
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: §506(a) measures secured interest by collateral, and §506(b) permits postpetition interest only oversecured lender within available cushion. §502(b)(2) general rule bars unmatured interest; undersecured creditor cannot sidestep via §362(d)(1).
entries.laymanExplanation: If Code says interest only for lenders with extra collateral, judge can't rename it 'protection' for underwater lenders.
entries.legalExplanation: Compare $4.366m debt with ≤$4.25m collateral, no cushion.
entries.examTrap: Case doesn't bar oversecured §506(b) postpetition interest, which is different statutory right.

entries.title: §552(b) postpetition rents/profits argument
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: §552(b) extends prefiling lien to postpetition rents/products/proceeds only when agreement and applicable nonbankruptcy perfection conditions satisfied; AP lost-income theory could effectively give rents to lenders lacking qualified lien.
entries.laymanExplanation: Can't get rent income security interest simply by asking for missed opportunity earnings.
entries.legalExplanation: This structural reason prevents evasion of limited postpetition proceeds protection.
entries.examApplication: In Problems 7.4–7.5 check contract + prepetition state-law perfection and §552 scope before AP.
entries.examTrap: Assignment of rents and enforceability are legally separate from general collateral interest.

entries.title: §362(d)(2) would be nullified by lender's theory
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: If undersecured lender always gets §362(d)(1) relief for lack of delayed-foreclosure interest, §362(d)(2)'s separate need to prove property not necessary to reorganization adds nothing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Without an interest-free breathing spell, even valuable reorganization collateral could be seized if debtor cannot pay hypothetical return.
entries.legalExplanation: Scalia saw two subsections as coordinated remedies: (d)(1) real value loss, (d)(2) lack of bankruptcy purpose.
entries.examApplication: Explain why first test isn't substitute for second test.
entries.examTrap: 'Bank underwater' doesn't automatically establish no adequate protection.

entries.title: Necessary for effective reorganization that is IN PROSPECT
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: To keep stay under (d)(2) debtor needs property for reorganization with reasonable possibility of success within reasonable time, not merely speculative future plan; debtor has proof burden per §362(g).
entries.laymanExplanation: Can't tell bank 'we may reorganize someday'; show actual plausible plan.
entries.legalExplanation: Early in exclusive plan drafting period judge can be more accommodating, but cannot ignore absence of any realistic prospect.
entries.examApplication: Use later Pegasus as application of dictum.
entries.examTrap: Timbers itself did not decide lender's (d)(2) eligibility on its facts.

entries.title: Adequate protection during stay vs plan interest at confirmation
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: §361 requires preservation of ability to realize collateral value at END of reorganization; §1129(b)(2)(A)(i)(II) and §1325 require PRESENT VALUE of future deferred plan payments AS OF plan effective date, with interest. Not identical clocks.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bank may wait through Chapter11 without interest for delay, but a later 5-year payment plan generally requires discounting interest.
entries.legalExplanation: Timbers rejects reading 'indubitable equivalent' in §361(3) as immediate interest duty; Till in Chapter6 deals confirmation rate.
entries.examApplication: In essay explicitly divide preconfirmation stay stage from postconfirmation cash stream.
entries.examTrap: No interest during stay does not imply no interest on later installment plan.

entries.title: Who wins and loses from no opportunity-cost compensation?
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: Debtor/DIP obtains temporary low-cost use of undersecured pledged assets for potential reorganization; lender loses chance to reinvest foreclosure proceeds, but still receives lien-value protection against actual decline.
entries.laymanExplanation: Business gains breathing room; bank sacrifices use of cash temporarily.
entries.legalExplanation: Bankruptcy distributes costs of rescue differently from normal lending, within Code's choice.
entries.examApplication: When professor policy asks whose ox is gored identify reorganization stakeholders and lender.
entries.examTrap: Do not state secured lenders have no protected property rights.

entries.title: Special SARE and family-farm exceptions in casebook context
entries.source: Uploaded Tabb & Brubaker Chapter 7 §B.2, complete excerpts of In re Alyucan Interstate Corp. (1981) and United Savings Assn v Timbers of Inwood Forest (1988), with casebook questions
entries.summary: Timbers general no-opportunity-compensation differs from explicit §362(d)(3) SARE alternative interest payments or §1205(b)(3) family farm adequate protection reasonable rent when applicable.
entries.laymanExplanation: New Code sections can require rent-like payments when ordinary AP would not.
entries.legalExplanation: Source links response to Congress's concerns over single-building delay abuse.
entries.examApplication: When debtor realty possibly SARE, analyze §101(51B) threshold.
entries.examTrap: Not every apartment project qualifies by name alone without statutory definition.
